title: Group Anagrams
corePattern: Hashing by Canonical Key - Equivalence Class Grouping
interviewTips: Ask if strings contain only lowercase English letters or Unicode - this decides between 26-count array vs sorting vs generic Counter key.
Clarify that order does not matter: any order of groups and any order inside groups is accepted.
Trade-off: sorted key is simpler and general O(K log K); counting key is O(K) per string and optimal under lowercase constraint.
Cover edge cases: empty input, single string, empty strings, duplicates, all anagrams vs no anagrams, and very long strings.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Pairwise Comparison
approaches.intuition: If two strings are anagrams they have identical character frequencies. Pick the first ungrouped string as a representative, scan all later ungrouped strings and pull those that are anagrams of it into the same group, then repeat.
approaches.theory: Define equivalence relation: a ~ b if isAnagram(a,b). We build equivalence classes greedily. isAnagram is checked in O(K) by counting 26 letters: increment for a, decrement for b, all zero means anagram. Each string is compared to at most N representatives, giving N^2 comparisons in worst case. This is correct but repeats counting work many times instead of hashing once.

timeComplexity.explanation: N strings, up to O(N^2) pairs checked, each isAnagram costs O(K) for length K to build 26-counts. Worst case when no anagrams.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Output stores all strings plus O(26)=O(1) temp freq per check and O(N) visited array.

dryRunExample.input: strs = [eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat]
steps: i=0 eat unvisited -> group=[eat], compare tea: anagram -> add, tan: no, ate: anagram -> add, nat: no, bat: no => [eat,tea,ate]
i=1 tea visited skip, i=2 tan unvisited -> group=[tan], ate visited skip, nat: anagram -> add, bat: no => [tan,nat]

approaches.name: Approach 2: Sorted String as Hash Key
approaches.intuition: Anagrams become identical when sorted. Use the sorted version of each string as a canonical key in a hash map, all strings sharing the same key belong to the same group.
approaches.theory: Sorting is a canonicalization function f where f(s1)==f(s2) iff s1 and s2 are anagrams. Hash map from key to list gives O(1) average grouping per string. This works for any comparable characters including Unicode, no alphabet size assumption needed. Cost is dominated by sorting each string of length K.

timeComplexity.explanation: N strings, sorting each length-K string costs O(K log K). Hash map operations O(K) to hash key average.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Hash map stores N strings plus sorted keys of total O(N*K) characters.

dryRunExample.input: strs = [eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat]

edgeCases: All distinct: [abc, def, ghi] => three singleton groups
Unicode strings still work with sorting

approaches.name: Approach 3: Character Frequency Count as Hash Key
approaches.intuition: Instead of sorting, count letters a-z. Two anagrams have identical 26-length frequency vectors, so use that vector as hash key. Counting is linear in string length.
approaches.theory: For lowercase English constraint, frequency vector of size 26 is a canonical form computable in O(K). Encode as tuple in Python, delimited string or array in C++/Java for hashing. Each string processed once: O(K) to count + O(26) to build key. Optimal when alphabet Sigma is small and fixed. Generalizes to larger alphabets with HashMap of counts but 26-array is fastest here.

timeComplexity.explanation: N strings, each needs O(K) to count characters plus O(26)=O(1) to build key. Hash insert O(1) average.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Map stores all N strings. Keys add O(N*26)=O(N) overhead. Counting array O(26)=O(1) per iteration.

dryRunExample.input: strs = [eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat]
steps: tea -> same counts -> same key -> group1=[eat,tea]

edgeCases: Empty string '' -> all-zero count key, all empties group together
Long strings length 100: counting stays linear, sorting would be slower
Requires lowercase a-z; for uppercase or Unicode use sorting or generic Counter key
